sections.html:
• Maximum length: 1.8 cm, the smallest species of the genus Nannostomus.
  • Origin: Venezuela (upper Orinoco) and northern Brazil (Rio Negro area).
  • Described by Fernandez & Weitzman, 1987.

Within the family Lebiasinidae, sixteen scientifically accepted species of the genus Nannostomus are known. In aquatic specialist shops only seven are usually offered: N. beckfordi, N. harrisoni, N. marginatus, N. mortenthaleri, N. trifasciatus, and the two 'head-ups' N. eques and N. unifasciatus; occasionally N. digrammus, N. espei and N. limatus are also available. N. britskii is completely unknown to the aquatic world.

Every now and then, some specimens of N. anduzei come as accidental catches to Europe. It can sometimes be found in catches of the Blue Neon, Paracheirodon simulans. Very often the fish are ignored due to their smallness.

The reference specimens come from a freshwater lagoon about 15 km north of Puerto Ayacucho, in the upper Rio Orinoco region of Venezuela. A second location is in northern Brazil, in the waters of a savanna in the Rio Negro area, belonging to the Rio Ererê, which flows from the north into the Rio Negro about 250 km northwest of the mouth of the Rio Branco, near the Rio Padauari. Imported fish probably come from the Rio Ererê region.

The water temperature in the Venezuelan lagoon was nearly 30 °C, with pH ranging from 5.0 to 7.0. The Brazilian site is one of the so-called 'black water' regions. Fish caught there have the same colouration as the Venezuelan specimens, but the males of the Brazilian form have a much longer anal fin.
Only a small aquarium with a volume of about 10 to 30 litres is needed.
At 27 °C, pH 7 or slightly below and 10 °dH hardness, the fish are absolutely unproblematic to keep.
Due to the smallness of the fish, use very fine, sieved Cyclops, sometimes small Grindal worms or artemia nauplii. Occasionally they also enjoy fine dry food.

Keep a shoal. Under suitable conditions, the males soon show courtship: the dominant males display a blood red caudal fin base and anal fin, the golden horizontal bar shines light green, and the brown back and the brown band below the gold-green bar turn grey-brown.

N. anduzei differs from all other Nannostomus species in lacking dark spots or bars in night colouration; at night the fish seem transparent with a golden shine, and the red in the anal fin and caudal base is hardly recognisable. Males of the Brazilian form have a much longer anal fin.

Courtship was often observed but the fish never spawned in the general tank. A group of four males and six females, selected from several Blue Neon imports, was placed in an 8 litre breeding tank: two thirds of the bottom was covered with Java moss and the surface with Ceratopteris. The spring water had pH 6.3 and 2 °dH hardness. The group was kept like this for ten days and fed artemia nauplii daily. Food remains accumulated in the light front part of the tank and were sucked out every two days. Afterwards the tank was filled up with fresh spring water.

Three days after the adults were removed, tiny eggs were seen stuck to the panes. They were 3 mm long, grey-white and very thin, with the head and clearly visible eye thicker than the rest of the body. Every two days two drops of Liquifry were added. At the beginning of the third week some artemia nauplii were added. After three weeks all plants were removed; only six young fish were present, now 4 mm long and considerably heavier. They were then seen eating nauplii. Some mud was sucked out, the tank was filled with spring water, and several ramshorn snails were added to eat food remains.

The first breeding was not very successful in numbers, but showed that breeding in the aquarium is possible. The species might, like many relatives, eat its own eggs; if so, breeding in pairs may be wiser.
